passed.title: `~selector` selects the other columns; it does not negate boolean values
passed.trap: On a selector, `~` is a set complement. `~cs.boolean()` means "every column that is not boolean". It does not flip true/false the way `~` does on a boolean `pl.col`. In the same way, `cs.all() - cs.numeric()` is a set difference of columns, not arithmetic. To invert the values in the boolean columns, call an expression method on the selector, such as `cs.boolean().not_()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"n": [1, 2], "flag": [True, False]})

# Set complement: picks the NON-boolean columns
print(df.select(~cs.boolean()).columns)

# Value negation of the boolean columns
print(df.select(cs.boolean().not_()))

# Set difference of columns, not subtraction
print(df.select(cs.all() - cs.numeric()).columns)

passed.title: A selector that matches nothing silently returns an empty frame
passed.trap: If no column matches a selector, `DataFrame.select` returns a `shape: (0, 0)` frame instead of raising. For example, `cs.list(cs.integer())` on a `list[str]` column, or `cs.array(width=3)` on width-2 arrays, gives an empty result. Downstream code then quietly works on nothing. These nested and enum selectors are also marked unstable. Check what matched with `cs.expand_selector` before relying on the result.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"tags": [["a"], ["b", "c"]], "n": [1, 2]})

sel = cs.list(cs.integer())  # inner type is str, so nothing matches
print(df.select(sel).shape)  # (0, 0), no error

matched = cs.expand_selector(df, sel)
print(matched)
if not matched:
    print("guard: no columns matched, falling back")
    sel = cs.list(cs.string())
print(df.select(sel).columns)
passed.output:
(0, 0)
()
guard: no columns matched, falling back
['tags']

passed.title: `cs.temporal` also matches time-of-day columns, not just dates
passed.trap: `cs.temporal` selects every temporal dtype, including `time` columns, not only date-like ones. Calendar operations applied through it, such as extracting the year, will hit `time` columns that have no date part. When you mean calendar dates, select them explicitly with `cs.date()` (combined with `cs.datetime()` if needed). Alternatively, remove times with `cs.temporal() - cs.time()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs
from datetime import date, time

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "dt": [date(2021, 1, 1), date(2022, 6, 2)],
    "tm": [time(12, 0), time(20, 30)],
})

print(df.select(cs.temporal()).columns)  # includes 'tm'
print(df.select(cs.temporal() - cs.time()).columns)
print(df.select(cs.date().dt.year()))

passed.title: `cs.numeric` skips boolean columns and `cs.float` skips decimals
passed.trap: Boolean columns are not numeric for selectors. So `cs.numeric().sum()` silently drops flag columns that a pandas user might expect to be counted. Likewise, `cs.float` only matches Float32/Float64. Decimal columns (for example money values) need `cs.decimal`. Combine selectors explicitly, such as `cs.numeric() | cs.boolean()` or `cs.float() | cs.decimal()`, when you want those columns included.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs
from decimal import Decimal

df = pl.DataFrame({"qty": [1, 2], "ok": [True, True]})
print(df.select(cs.numeric()).columns)  # 'ok' missing
print(df.select((cs.numeric() | cs.boolean()).cast(pl.Int64).sum()))

money = pl.DataFrame({
    "w": [0.5, 1.0],
    "price": [Decimal("1.50"), Decimal("2.25")],
})
print(money.select(cs.float()).columns)  # 'price' missing
print(money.select(cs.float() | cs.decimal()).columns)
